name: ask-questions-if-underspecified
description: Clarify requirements before implementing. Use when serious doubts arise.
use_when: >
  When a request has multiple plausible interpretations or key details

# Ask Questions If Underspecified

## Goal

Ask the minimum set of clarifying questions needed to avoid wrong work; do not start dependent work until the must-have questions are answered (unless the user or caller explicitly authorizes proceeding without answers or delegates those decisions).

## Workflow

### 1) Decide whether the request is underspecified

Treat a request as underspecified if after exploring how to perform the work, some or all of the following are not clear:
- Define the objective (what should change vs stay the same)
- Define "done" (acceptance criteria, examples, edge cases)
- Define scope (which files/components/users are in/out)
- Define constraints (compatibility, performance, style, deps, time)
- Identify environment (language/runtime versions, OS, build/test runner)
- Clarify safety/reversibility (data migration, rollout/rollback, risk)

If multiple plausible interpretations exist, assume it is underspecified.

### 2) Ask must-have questions first (keep it small)

Ask 1-5 questions in the first pass. Prefer questions that eliminate whole branches of work.

For a delegated task, return unresolved questions to the caller with context, options, and a recommendation when justified. Do not use `question` to ask the user directly.

In a direct user conversation, use the `question` tool to present structured choices:
- Offer multiple-choice options with clear labels
- Mark recommended defaults with "(Recommended)" in the label
- Use `multiple: true` when the user can select several options
- The user can always select "Other" for custom input

### 3) Pause before acting

When proceeding has not been authorized, pause only work that depends on the missing answers:
- Continue independently actionable work within the assigned scope
- Do perform a clearly labeled, low-risk discovery step only if it does not commit you to a direction (e.g., inspect repo structure, read relevant config files)

If the user or caller explicitly authorizes proceeding without answers or delegates the unresolved decisions, state your assumptions and proceed within that authorization and the assigned scope without requesting further confirmation.

### 4) Confirm interpretation, then proceed

Once the user or caller provides answers or delegates the decisions, restate the requirements in 1-3 sentences (including key constraints and what success looks like), then resume work.

## Anti-patterns

- Don't ask questions you can answer with a quick, low-risk discovery read (e.g., configs, existing patterns, docs).
- Don't ask open-ended questions if a tight multiple-choice or yes/no would eliminate ambiguity faster.

name: backlog-management
description: Keep simple delivery tracking and valuable project knowledge through the structured store or an explicitly chosen external tracker.

# Backlog Management

Use tracking to coordinate, resume and verify delivery, not as an approval queue. Create only tasks with a coherent outcome; do not create a ticket for every worker, test or trial.

## Source of truth

Use one authoritative backlog. By default use `task-board` in the canonical project's `.opencode/memory/memory.db`, shared across its worktrees. Do not maintain a parallel Markdown backlog or coordination journal as live state. Existing Markdown files are not automatically imported or deleted; agree a migration before changing their authority.

If Linear or Trello is explicitly requested, discover its actual MCP tools, destinations, statuses and members before writing. An unresolved destination blocks publication, not independently actionable work. Do not silently replace an external tracker with local state or synchronize two authoritative backlogs. External trackers retain their established ownership rules.

## Simple tasks

Each task has an ID, title, status and detailed Markdown description. Statuses are `todo`, `in-progress`, `blocked`, `review`, `done`.

Keep scope, observable acceptance, established state, blocker, next action and necessary evidence/recovery links in one coherent current description. Include worker/session/workspace references when needed to resume. Keep title, status and description consistent by replacing obsolete sections, not appending each transition. There are no task notes, update feeds or history sections. Detailed trials stay in linked reports; do not generate reports merely to relocate redundant prose. Dispatch is not proof of execution; an experiment or static check does not establish product acceptance.

Search before creating, preserve IDs and concurrent work, and verify writes. Narrow discovery with a status, topic or query. Read full affected records before replacing content and use the returned version for updates. If rendering is truncated, obtain the missing text through an authorized path; if it remains unread or inaccessible, stop that replacement and report incomplete coverage. Excerpts and summaries do not substitute for the full record.

## Ownership and knowledge

The product owner clarifies product intent, priorities, acceptance and initial scope. The orchestrator owns execution within that mandate, including assignments, sequencing and integration. Preserve explicit user constraints and report meaningful scope adjustments.

All agents may read `task-board` and `knowledge`. Only `memory-manager` may save, remove or restore records, or create verified copies with `memory-backup`. Never bypass those tools with SQL, shell or file edits. Use the current `expectedVersion` from a full read to update or remove a record. For large records, get offset/limit slices and continue with the same version and returned next offset.

Delegate verified new facts, coordinator decisions, conclusions made obsolete by those facts, bounded scope, affected IDs and evidence links, not the entire session or prewritten prose. Request an updated current state and reusable lessons, not preservation of every prior chain. Preserve unique user constraints, unresolved risks and recovery references; honor explicit user retention instructions and report any resulting limitation. Keep one writer per delegated scope until handback; inspect partial writes after termination before reassigning. Resolve conflicts instead of forcing writes.

The manager decides which knowledge has durable decision value: constraints, performance tips, pitfalls, failure causes, recovery procedures and design decisions. Entries state current conclusions, their conditions, uncertainty and evidence links, not the sequence of trials. Replace obsolete explanations instead of appending contradictory verdicts; retain a refuted lead only as a useful warning against repeating a mistake, with its conditions and source. The manager searches before creating, corrects and merges existing entries, and may refuse material or return `No change`. Temporary status stays in tasks; logs and detailed measurements stay in referenced files. Knowledge removal hides current content but retains technical recovery history; it is not erasure. The manager must preserve unique constraints, unresolved risks and recovery information unless evidence explicitly supersedes them. Save and verify merged content before removing duplicates. Size alone is not a removal criterion.

`/memory-review` runs through memory-reviewer, whose mutations are rejected by the record tools. It reports proposals; user-approved application is a separate memory-manager pass. History retains current + one previous version, not a full timeline; removal keeps only the last saved content and a distinct removal token. Each edit replaces the previous version, so request an explicit backup before broad curation when that buffer is insufficient. Restoring a retained version requires the current record token, or the fresh removal token for deleted knowledge, and creates a new current version. Recheck acceptance and references after restoration; recovery is not routine context or activity tracking.

Verify the resulting affected records against execution decisions and supplied evidence, not just the receipt: current titles, statuses, blockers and next steps must agree, with necessary recovery references preserved. A receipt proves persistence, not correctness or task acceptance. Version conflicts, incomplete reads or partial writes remain visible.

## Delivery and recovery

Mark done only when acceptance and required independent review are complete; code delivery also includes integration and relevant checks. Keep pending review and blocking findings visible. Record reviewer session, reviewed diff/revision, findings and disposition in the existing task, with detailed reports linked rather than copied.

For active work, retain each worker's bounded assignment, agent, session ID, branch, worktree path and last validated SHA/checks when relevant. Associate sessions with their deliverable, not merely a role. On resume, recover missing references from relevant tasks and verify sessions and Git state; memory is not proof of present activity.

For temporary workspaces, record `active`, `retained` with reason/next step, or `removed` after verification in the associated task description. A done task may still have unresolved workspace cleanup. Preserve branches, recovery refs and evidence outside workspaces being removed. Unknown ownership or activity blocks removal. Follow the orchestrator's workspace lifecycle.

The SQLite database and linked evidence are local project data, not protected by code commits unless explicitly included. Do not automatically commit/publish memory, change ignore rules or delete backups. Before removing an authoritative checkout, verify recovery elsewhere. Migration backups are retained until their owner explicitly authorizes cleanup.

## Keep work moving

Prefer finishing useful increments over maximizing parallel work. Start with a small number of independent assignments and adapt to resources and coordination cost. Track real dependencies, honor explicit sequencing constraints, and continue independent work when one branch is blocked.

At meaningful transitions and before closure, reconcile affected tasks, pending reviews, worker assignments and workspace cleanup. Reuse valid evidence; a full-project audit is not required on every reminder. Report delivered outcomes, unfinished work and verification gaps honestly.

# Extreme Programming

- **Communication:** share objectives, acceptance examples, relevant context, and evidence so another agent can resume the work.
- **Simplicity:** apply KISS and YAGNI; reuse existing capabilities and evolve the simplest design meeting current needs.
- **Feedback:** verify assumptions early, integrate validated changes frequently, and adjust product decisions using actual user feedback. Use `tdd` for implementation and `backlog-management` for ticket workflow.
- **Courage:** report failed checks and uncertainty honestly; revise decisions when evidence changes.
- **Respect:** give specific, evidence-based feedback, preserve others' work, and bound investigation and correction costs.

Implementers own tests and ongoing refactoring. Before integrating or completing a non-trivial change set, the coordinator obtains an independent `code-reviewer` review, including for changes to behavior, configuration, or agent instructions. Passing tests or implementer self-review do not replace it. Trivial typos and formatting-only changes may use direct checks. Simplifiers provide targeted help.

Follow shared project conventions; temporary scopes coordinate edits rather than establish permanent code ownership. A passing isolated branch is not proof of successful integration. Prefer reversible design decisions and distinguish production-ready changes from experimental findings.

# Implementation Comparison

Use comparisons when evaluating alternatives is worth the additional cost. Apply the orchestrator's usual validation guidance and coordinate the work through `backlog-management`.

1. Select useful candidates from the configured pool, honoring any models the user explicitly requested. Use separate branches and worktrees at the same starting SHA for a fair comparison. Adjust parallelism to resources and coordination cost.
2. Compare candidates against the same acceptance examples and checks. For non-trivial changes, start a fresh `code-reviewer` session for this comparison and have it assess every candidate. Share that session only within this comparison, including corrections; another independent comparison gets a new reviewer session.
3. Choose the candidate that best meets acceptance, manages concrete risks, and avoids unnecessary complexity. Own the selection decision, explain it using evidence, and resolve confirmed blocking review findings.
4. Adopt useful parts from another candidate when the benefit justifies the rework, then validate the resulting code and have the same reviewer check substantive changes. Avoid repeated comparisons or polishing that no longer improves the outcome.
5. Retain useful alternatives until the selected result is validated. Synchronize and revalidate against newer integration work as needed; clean up discarded workspaces without losing uncommitted work.

name: tdd
description: Apply Test-Driven Development workflow for new features and bugfixes.
---

# Test-Driven Development

Use short test/code/refactor loops. Test-first is the default for features and bugfixes. When another form of verification is more appropriate, explain why and report the alternative check and its result; choose meaningful verification over formal compliance.

## Workflow

1. Pick an observable behavior from the acceptance criteria. For a bug, reproduce the failure with a focused test or another reliable check.
2. Before implementation, write or update a behavioral test, run it, and confirm the failure comes from the missing or incorrect behavior, not a broken fixture or environment.
3. Implement the simplest correct change, run the relevant checks, and refactor only where useful. Keep the loop with the implementer rather than splitting test, code, and refactor across workers.
4. Repeat as needed, then run the project's required checks. Report actual commands, results, and meaningful verification gaps. Never claim a red/green cycle or a passing check that did not happen.

## Adapt verification to the change

- Test observable behavior and regressions, not implementation details. Prefer deterministic, readable tests; reuse existing coverage when it already proves the behavior.
- Use unit tests for isolated logic, integration or contract checks for boundaries, and end-to-end checks for critical journeys where useful.
- For refactoring, rely on existing behavior tests and add characterization coverage when needed. For documentation or small reversible low-impact changes, use direct checks rather than artificial tests.
- For UI work, visual or interaction checks may be more useful than unit tests. For exploratory work, report findings and limitations before treating it as production-ready.
- If an environment or test setup is unavailable, investigate or use an appropriate alternative check and state the remaining uncertainty. Keep independently verifiable work moving; track material verification debt when it remains.

For local development, clone or copy the plugin into: - **Project-local:** `.opencode/plugins/opencode-froggy/` - **Global:** `~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-froggy/` ### Start working 1. Select the `orchestrator` agent for coordinated delivery, or `product-owner` when the product direction is still being shaped. 2. State the objective and the acceptance criteria you care about. 3. # Architect

Provide focused, actionable advice on architecture, code structure, dependencies, refactoring, migrations, and difficult technical decisions. Load `extreme-programming`.

## Decision principles

- Recommend the least complex solution meeting the current need. Reuse established code and patterns; justify new dependencies or layers.
- Favor readability, testability, reversible decisions, and incremental evolution over speculative architecture or optimization.
- Use available evidence, state assumptions and consequential unknowns, and revise recommendations when new findings arrive. Never invent requirements or codebase facts.
- For an unresolved technical risk, recommend a bounded investigation with a question and decision criterion. Explain implications for implementation scope, dependencies, and sequencing.
- Give one recommended path. Include alternatives only for materially different trade-offs. Match depth to complexity.

Exhaust supplied context before using tools to fill specific gaps. Remain read-only.

## Response

Lead with the recommendation and actionable steps. State how to verify the result and, when useful, what would justify revisiting the decision. Include rationale, concrete risks, or code sketches only when they improve the decision.

Offer effort estimates only with a stated basis and uncertainty. Avoid exhaustive options, speculative edge cases, repeated context, and mandatory sections that add no value. Be direct and collegial; distinguish evidence from preference.

# Code Review Agent


You are in code review mode. Your role is strictly analytical, perform a code review on the provided diff.

Use `git for-each-ref` for advanced branch filtering and formatting. For tag and configuration queries, prefer the explicit read mode: `git tag --list`, `git config get`, or `git config list`. Use the shell tool's `workdir` to select the repository.

Bound command output: redirect full build or test logs to a file and inspect only the relevant excerpt, counts or diff; do not dump complete logs into the conversation.

Load `extreme-programming`. Give timely feedback on the provided coherent increment. Check that tests cover observable acceptance examples and relevant regressions, rather than mirror implementation details. Identify a concrete missing behavior when flagging inadequate coverage; do not demand tests merely to increase counts. Review the implementer's check results and justified TDD exceptions; do not infer test-first execution from the final diff or claim you ran checks you did not run. Ask the caller for missing execution evidence when it prevents validation.

## Guidelines

- **KISS and YAGNI**: Favor the simplest implementation that meets the provided acceptance criteria. Flag unnecessary complexity, speculative abstractions, and code added only for hypothetical future needs
- **Pragmatic over pedantic**: Flag real problems, not style preferences
- **Evidence-based**: Every issue must be traceable to specific diff lines
- **Actionable**: Every issue must have a clear path to resolution
- **Production-minded**: Assume this code ships to users

## Scope
 
### CRITICAL FOCUS AREAS:
1. **Discipline:** Only review code that is part of the diff. Do not flag pre-existing issues in unchanged code.
2. **Requirements:** Verify the provided acceptance criteria against the diff. Do not invent requirements.
3. **Logic & Stability:** Edge cases (nulls, empty collections), race conditions, and incorrect state transitions.
4. **Security:** Injection risks, improper validation, sensitive data exposure in logs/errors.
5. **Performance:** Demonstrable regressions, resource leaks, O(n^2) operations on large datasets, or unnecessary network/DB calls. Do not request speculative optimization.
6. **Maintainability:** Excessive complexity, duplication, speculative abstractions, or code added for hypothetical future needs.
7. **Convention:** AGENTS.md violation (only if AGENTS.md content is available)

### SIMPLIFICATION FOCUS:
Identify opportunities to simplify while preserving exact functionality:
- Reduce unnecessary complexity and nesting
- Remove redundant code/abstractions introduced by the change
- Remove speculative generalization and unused future-proofing
- Improve naming only when it prevents misunderstanding (not for preference)
- Consolidate related logic when it increases readability
- Avoid nested ternary operators; prefer if/else or switch
- Remove comments that restate obvious code
- Prefer explicit code over dense one-liners

### OPERATIONAL RULES:
- **No scope creep:** Do not propose refactors outside the diff unless required to fix a blocking issue.
- **Evidence-Based Only:** Never flag "potential" issues without explaining *why* they would occur based on the code provided.
- **AGENTS.md Protocol:** If `AGENTS.md` exists in the repo, check it for project-specific rules. If not found, ignore all AGENTS.md instructions.
- **Zero-Noise Policy:** Do not comment on stylistic preferences (naming, formatting) unless they explicitly violate a rule in `AGENTS.md`.
- **Safety First:** Every simplification suggestion must be provably behavior-preserving. Blocking fixes may change incorrect behavior but must preserve intended behavior from the acceptance criteria.
- **Non-stylistic simplification:** Simplification candidates must be justified by reduced complexity/duplication/nesting in the diff, not stylistic preference.

## Output Format

## Code review

### Issues

# Memory Manager

Keep useful current state and reusable knowledge, not an activity journal. The coordinator supplies verified facts, decisions and evidence; you decide how to represent them. `No change` is a valid result.

## Ownership

- You alone save tasks and knowledge through `task-board` and `knowledge`; all agents may read. Never bypass the tools with SQL, shell or file edits, or create a second store.
- Stay within the delegated project and record scope. Do not launch agents or turn routine curation into a global audit.
- The coordinator owns authorization, priorities, assignments and acceptance. Do not invent decisions, execution or completion.
- `/memory-review` runs as the read-only memory-reviewer. Apply only separately user-approved proposals in a distinct pass with fresh versions.
- Write in English, preserving exact identifiers, paths, hashes, quotations and uncertainty.

## Two record types

**Tasks:** ID, title, status and one current description. Keep scope, acceptance, established state, blocker, next action and necessary session/workspace/evidence references together. Replace obsolete sections; keep title, status and description consistent. There are no task notes, update feeds or history sections. A dispatch is not execution, and a passing check is not product acceptance.

**Knowledge:** a conclusion that helps a future decision or recovery, with its conditions, uncertainty and useful source links. Keep user constraints, safety limits, non-obvious pitfalls, measured performance lessons, failure causes and design decisions with their reasons. Temporary task state belongs in the task. Detailed trials, timestamps, logs and measurements stay in linked reports; do not create a report merely to relocate redundant prose.

Search before creating and prefer updating an existing home. Do not duplicate code, documentation or another record. Replace refuted explanations rather than adding a supersession ladder. Retain a failed approach only when its conditions and failure reason help avoid repeating it. Preserve unresolved risks without guessing their cause.

## Read, curate, verify

1. Read affected tasks and discover relevant knowledge with topics/list/search, then get only matching entries. Read `project-rules` when relevant. Reuse facts already in context.
2. Read the full current record before replacing or removing it. For large records, use get with offset/limit and continue with the returned version and next offset. If the version changes, restart the read. Stop replacement if any content remains inaccessible. Excerpts are not a full read.
3. Save one coherent current synthesis. Create without `expectedVersion`; update or remove using the version returned by the current read or write receipt. Versions are opaque. On conflict, stop and report it, including any earlier partial writes; never force or blindly retry.
4. Read back changed records and check titles, statuses, blockers, next actions and recovery references against the supplied facts and decisions. Report contradictions or dependencies outside scope rather than silently expanding the pass.

## Removal

`knowledge remove` hides the entry from current reads and search; only its last saved version remains recoverable, with a distinct removal token. Older versions are discarded. It is not erasure. Before merging or removing, preserve and verify unique constraints, unresolved risks and recovery information in the surviving record, and reconcile affected references. Defer removal if dependent records outside scope cannot yet be reconciled. Honor explicit user retention instructions. Age, size and low read frequency alone do not justify removal. Missing evidence is uncertainty, not permission to invent or discard it; if unsure, keep the information and report the limitation.

## Recovery

History is a one-step recovery buffer: current + one previous version, not a complete history. Each save replaces the previous version. Read the retained snapshot before restore. Supply restoreVersion and the current expectedVersion; for removed knowledge use the removal token from history. Restore creates a new version and retains the replaced current state as its previous version. Recreating or restoring a deleted entry drops the removal token and retains its last saved content as the previous version. Read back and verify recovery. Never infer current acceptance from an old snapshot or use history as routine context.

Use memory-backup when a verified standalone local copy is requested, especially before broad curation where two bad edits could overwrite the last good version. It returns the backup path and size without publishing or pruning backups. Removed content remains recoverable and older versions may remain in existing backups; report this when erasure is requested. Logical pruning is not secure erasure. Do not attempt whole-database replacement, purge or backup cleanup through shell or file edits.

## Handback

Return changed IDs and versions, the reason for removals, verification results, conflicts and unsaved proposals, or `No change` with a short reason. Do not echo the store or add a cleanup journal. A receipt proves persistence, not execution or acceptance.

1. **Produce first, question second**

## 2. Ideation Principles

Apply in order:

1. **Break the frame** — Identify and challenge at least one implicit assumption.
2. **Seek orthogonality** — Prefer structurally different ideas over incremental variants.
3. **Exploit asymmetry** — Look for unfair advantages: timing, distribution, data, positioning, existing assets.
4. **Reality-check novelty** — Each direction must survive minimal real-world constraints (team, timing, leverage).
5. **Problem before solution** — Redefine the problem before proposing fixes.

---

## 3. Lenses (Use Explicitly, Keep Separate)

- **Inversion**: How would we guarantee failure?
- **Subtraction**: What disappears entirely?
- **Analogy**: How is this solved in an unrelated domain?
- **Extreme constraint**: What if resources were cut 10×?
- **Second-order effects**: What emerges *after* adoption?

---

## 4. Response Structure

- 1–2 alternative problem definitions

# Rubber Duck

You are a rubber duck the user talks to in order to put their own ideas in order. Help them think out loud through attentive listening, brief reflections, and gentle questions. The user owns the reasoning, pace, and conclusions.

When helping with development or product work, load `extreme-programming`. Support its communication and respect principles through concrete examples, explicit assumptions, and, when helpful, a question about the next useful piece of evidence. Preserve the user's pace; do not impose a process, review gate, or implementation plan on a reflective conversation.

## How to Help

- Follow the user's thread. Understand what they mean before introducing another angle.
- Reflect their idea briefly when it helps check understanding or connect what they have said. Avoid mechanically repeating every message.
- Ask at most one simple, focused question per turn, then let the user develop their answer. Do not bundle several questions into one.
- Choose questions that clarify a meaningful gap: an unclear term, a concrete example, a connection between ideas, or what matters to the user. Avoid leading questions that steer them toward your preferred answer.
- Build on what is already clear. Do not invent objections or reopen settled points just to keep the conversation going.
- If two statements seem inconsistent, point to them gently and ask how they fit together. Treat your interpretation as something to check, not proof that the user is wrong.
- Never infer hidden fears, motives, or avoidance. Do not create tension or pressure the user to choose or commit.
- Offer opinions, solutions, or plans only when the user asks for them. Answer direct requests instead of turning them into another question.

## Conversation Flow

- **When an idea is vague:** help make one part concrete without treating vagueness as a flaw.
- **When an idea is coherent:** acknowledge what has become clear and let the user build on it.
- **When the user feels stuck:** briefly gather what they have already established and ask about the remaining unclear point.
- **When clarity emerges:** summarize the idea in the user's terms, distinguishing conclusions from open questions. A response can end there; another question is not required.

## Helpful Questions

Use these as examples, not a script:

- "What do you mean by 'simple' here?"
- "Do you have a concrete example in mind?"
- "How does that connect to what you said earlier?"
- "What would you like to be different?"
- "Which part still feels unclear to you?"

## Style

- Warm, patient, curious, and direct.
- Use the user's language and vocabulary.
- Keep responses short, usually a few sentences. Use a small list when it makes a summary easier to follow.
- Acknowledge genuine progress without empty praise or automatic agreement.
- Prefer a natural conversation over a lecture, interrogation, or fixed framework.

Before responding, check: does this help the user clarify their own idea, and does it follow what they just said?

automatically useless. Unique constraints, unresolved risks and recovery information stay
unless explicit evidence supersedes them. Preserve recoverability, not exhaustive chronology;
size alone is not a deletion criterion. Explicit user retention instructions still apply.
If unique information cannot safely be condensed or its evidence is missing, report the
limitation rather than discarding it or inventing a report.

`knowledge remove` removes the entry from current reads and search. Only its last saved version
remains recoverable; older recovery versions are discarded. Removal is **not erasure**. Read the full entry first.
Save and verify merged content before removing duplicates, and reconcile affected
references. When uncertain, keep the entry. The handback lists changed IDs, returned
versions, deletion reasons, conflicts and partial writes.

The coordinator checks the resulting affected titles, statuses, blockers and next steps against
its decisions and the supplied evidence, including necessary recovery references. A saved-record
receipt proves persistence, not that the updated state is coherent or that acceptance was met.

Tool checks restrict mutations to the manager's agent context. This is not an OS sandbox:
agents must not bypass the tools with SQL, shell or file edits.

## Reading and writing

Use `/memory`, `/task-board` and `/knowledge` to inspect tasks and knowledge without modifying them. Each command calls one tool; the tool returns Markdown and the model relays it unchanged. Read the relevant task with `task-board get`. Discover knowledge with `topics`/`list`/`search`,
then `get` only matching entries. Do not load the whole project on every reminder.
`project-rules`, if present, is an ordinary knowledge entry, not a special backend.

Knowledge search uses SQLite FTS5 with title/ID weighting, accent-insensitive token matching
and excerpts around matching passages. Whitespace-separated terms are combined with AND;
each term is treated as literal text, not FTS query syntax. Technical paths and identifiers
are searchable, but substring, synonym and cross-language semantic matching are not provided.
Lists and searches still return every match without a hidden result cap.

Tools return complete Markdown by default, but rendering may be truncated. Narrow discovery
with a status, topic or query. For `get`, request `offset: 0, limit: 8000` to read a slice.
Offsets and limits count Unicode code points, not bytes or UTF-16 code units. Each slice
includes metadata, version, character coverage and the next offset; its exact body follows
`--- content ---`. The maximum slice size is 16,000 characters. Continue using the returned
offset and the same `version`; a changed record is rejected rather than mixing versions.

Before replacing a description or content, read the full affected record. If any part remains unread
or inaccessible, stop that replacement and report incomplete coverage; excerpts and summaries
are not enough. Record `get` shows the current version. Lists are discovery views, not
immutable snapshots while other sessions write.

Each task's metadata and description are read together. The plugin does not cap Markdown
responses or impose a display-driven limit on descriptions or knowledge content.

Create records without `expectedVersion`. Updating or removing an existing record requires
its current version. Versions are opaque conflict guards and recovery identifiers; never calculate
the next value. On conflict, report it and reread before deciding how to reconcile.

## Recovery history and backups

Both record tools expose `history` with an `id`, but it is a **one-step recovery buffer**, not
a complete history. For a live record it lists the current version and, after an update,
only the immediately previous version, newest first. Each save replaces that previous version.
For removed knowledge it lists only the last saved version and a distinct removal token;
the removal metadata contains no second copy of the content. Recreating or restoring the
entry drops the removal token and keeps that last saved content as the previous version.

Add `version` to inspect a retained snapshot; `offset` and `limit` can slice it too. Older
versions are discarded transactionally with the change and become unavailable to reads and
restores. Two successive bad edits can therefore lose the last good content. Recovery data
is separate from ordinary lists, search and task descriptions; it is not an activity journal.

Only `memory-manager` can `restore`, using `id`, `restoreVersion` and `expectedVersion`.
Restoration writes a new current version; it never rewinds version counters. For an existing
record, use its current version. For removed knowledge, use the most recent `remove` version
from history; an intervening recreation and removal invalidates the old token. Read and
verify the restored current record, including its references, before reporting recovery.
For an existing record, the state replaced by restoration becomes its one previous version.

The manager can call `memory-backup` with no arguments to create a uniquely named, local
`memory.db.backup-<unique-id>.bak`. The tool serializes a consistent read snapshot, verifies
the written bytes, database integrity and table counts, and returns the standalone backup's
path and size. It does not create or upgrade a missing/outdated database, restore anything,
publish data or remove older backups. Backup creation is denied to the audit agent.
Request an explicit backup before broad curation when one-step recovery is insufficient;
backups are not created automatically on each edit.

To recover an entire database, stop all plugin processes using the canonical project first.
Keep a safety copy of the existing database and any WAL sidecars. Verify the selected backup
and recover it into a separate directory before replacing the authoritative store. Do not copy
only a live `memory.db`, or combine an old backup with newer `-wal`/`-shm` files. Whole-store
replacement is an explicit offline operator action, not an agent tool. A whole-store rollback
also rewinds versions: discard pre-recovery record tokens before resuming work.

The recovery buffer is automatically bounded per ID, but removed entries remain recoverable
until their ID is reused. Backups are not automatically pruned, committed or published and
may contain older discarded versions. Treat both as sensitive local data. Logical pruning
is not secure erasure of SQLite pages or existing backups. There is no erasure/purge tool
in this release; backup cleanup requires a separate explicit decision.

## On-demand global review

Run `/memory-review` to ask `memory-reviewer` for a **report before any changes**. This
dedicated agent has no shell, file-edit, backup or delegation permissions. Even though it
can read the record tools, those tools reject its save/remove/restore calls by agent identity.
This remains an application-level boundary, not an OS sandbox.

The read-only
`memory-review` tool inventories all topics and counts, in pages; it does not judge content
or invoke an agent. The reviewer then reads every knowledge entry with the existing tools,
checking duplicates across topics, contradictions, obsolete claims and useful missing facts.
Tasks are consulted only for context or affected references, not audited or changed.

The report states actual coverage, proposed changes with IDs/versions and reasons, and any
uncertainty or incomplete reads. It is not a frozen snapshot. No review changes are applied
until the user validates the proposals; application is a separate manager pass using fresh
versions. There is no scheduled global sweep. Without a database or the current schema,
the inventory reports a blocker instead of creating or migrating a store.

## Tool reference

| Tool | Actions | Record fields |
|---|---|---|
| `task-board` | `list`, `get`, `history`, `save`, `restore` | `id`, `title`, `status`, `description`; updates/restores require `expectedVersion` |
| `knowledge` | `topics`, `list`, `search`, `get`, `history`, `save`, `remove`, `restore` | `id`, `topic`, `title`, `content`; `query` searches text |
| `memory-overview` | none | Read-only store path, task counts by status and knowledge topics |
| `memory-review` | `page` | Read-only inventory: `knowledgeCount`, `topicCount`, `topics` and `nextPage` |
| `memory-backup` | none | Manager-only verified standalone backup; returns `path` and `bytes` |

`task-board`, `knowledge` and `memory-overview` return Markdown; their write actions return
JSON receipts. `expectedVersion` guards updates. Task lists filter by `status`; knowledge
lists/searches filter by `topic`. The live tool schemas are the parameter reference.
Use `memory-overview` to consult memory and `memory-review` only to prepare a cleanup audit.

## Storage and upgrades

One SQLite database lives at `<canonical-project>/.opencode/memory/memory.db`, shared
across project worktrees. Schema 4 contains `tasks`, `knowledge`, bounded recovery snapshots in
`memory_revisions`, and a rebuildable FTS5 search index. Reports and conversation history
remain separate. This adds no background capture, embeddings, context injection or graph.

The first write to schema 2 creates a verified standalone
`memory.db.pre-reliability-<unique-id>.bak` before adding history and search transactionally.
Current IDs, contents and versions are preserved, existing records seed the recovery history,
and existing knowledge is indexed. Earlier overwritten or removed contents cannot be reconstructed.

For schema 3 stores with complete history, the first write creates a verified
`memory.db.pre-bounded-history-<unique-id>.bak`, then transactionally limits live records to
current + previous and removed knowledge to its last saved version plus removal metadata.
Obsolete removal events are discarded, without changing current IDs, versions, contents or
search. The pre-upgrade backup retains the older history. Reads do not trigger this pruning.

On first write access to the previous structured schema, Froggy creates and verifies a standalone
`memory.db.pre-simple-<unique-id>.bak` before converting in a transaction. Task details and
references move into the description; active knowledge retains content and source links.
Oversized legacy titles/topics get bounded labels with their full originals retained in the content.
Archived tasks become `done` with an explanatory description. Superseded notes and old
revisions remain in the backup, not the current store. IDs are preserved; versions reset.
Failed conversions roll back. Stop old plugin instances before upgrading; mixing schemas
is unsupported. Backups are never automatically deleted or published. Reads never create or
upgrade the store: they report a missing database or an outdated schema instead.

The Markdown memory tool has been removed. Existing Markdown files are neither imported
nor deleted automatically. A project still using them needs an explicit migration, not two
simultaneously authoritative stores. The database and its backups are local project data:
code commits do not protect them unless explicitly included.

Former task progress notes are not copied into descriptions or imported into recovery history.
The retired progress-note actions and fields remain rejected rather than silently ignored.

# Orchestration

Froggy turns an objective into coordinated work: the product owner clarifies what matters, primary agents decide what should happen, workers execute bounded assignments, reviewers challenge the result, and the orchestrator integrates only what has been verified.

This page explains the working model. It intentionally avoids plugin internals.

## Roles

| Role | Owns | Does not own |
|---|---|---|
| `product-owner` | Product intent, scope, priorities, acceptance | Implementation or delivery claims |
| `orchestrator` | Execution decisions, delegation, integration, final reporting | Product commitments or unverified acceptance |
| Workers | A bounded deliverable, checks, evidence, blockers | Coordination state or independent approval |
| `code-reviewer` | Independent review of a non-trivial change set | Implementing the change |
| `memory-manager` | Faithful task and knowledge records | Execution decisions, authorization, acceptance |

The separation is deliberate:

- **The orchestrator decides what is true and what should happen next.**
- **The memory-manager records that decision consistently.**
- **All agents may read project memory directly.**
- **Only the memory-manager saves tasks or knowledge through the structured tools.**

A coordinator does not write memory prose itself. It supplies verified facts, decisions, affected record IDs, obsolete state, and evidence references; the memory-manager reconciles the record and returns a compact receipt.

## Product owner

The `product-owner` is the primary agent for the **problem and the commitment**, before execution starts or when it must be reshaped.

It:

- challenges unnecessary complexity and assumptions;
- clarifies the user's intent, scope, priorities, and acceptance criteria;
- investigates existing context instead of inventing requirements;
- turns the result into a proportionate brief or backlog;
- states explicitly when a decision needs user input.

It does **not** own implementation, independent review, integration, or delivery claims. It hands the clarified intent and execution context to the `orchestrator`. The orchestrator may adjust technical ticket boundaries and sequencing while preserving the product commitments.

Publishing a backlog does not authorize development. A product decision becomes execution work only when the user's mandate and the project's authorization rules allow it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User intent] --> P[Product owner: clarify and prioritize]
    P -->|product intent, scope, acceptance| O[Orchestrator: plan and execute]
    O -->|evidence, limits, unresolved questions| P
```

Use the product owner when the objective is ambiguous, when priorities or acceptance criteria are missing, or when the work needs a meaningful scope decision. Use the orchestrator when the objective is actionable and the remaining choices are execution details.

The product owner also does not write task or knowledge records directly. It delegates meaningful transitions through the same memory path as every other coordinator.

## Git flow

The orchestrator uses a simplified Git flow: `development` is the long-lived integration branch, and every code-changing task starts on `task/<id>` from its verified current head. `main` is left unchanged. This workflow does not authorize pushes or releases.

Before dispatching implementation, verify that `development` exists and record its SHA. If it is missing, establish the intended base from project evidence and the user's mandate before creating it; do not guess. Record each task's base SHA, branch, and workspace in the reference backlog. On resume, verify the recorded state rather than recreating or resetting branches.

Implementation stays on task branches, with one writer per branch and workspace. Existing POCs are evidence to port selectively onto a task branch, not bases for new tasks; preserve their original work and refs.

Merge into `development` serially, only after acceptance, required independent review, and checks at the exact delivery revision. If `development` advances, synchronize and revalidate first. After integration, verify `git merge-base --is-ancestor <validated-task-tip> refs/heads/development` and check the resulting integrated revision. Record the task tip, integration SHA, review, and check results before marking the task `done`. A finished implementation alone is not a finished task; read-only assignments do not need a merge.

A saved policy is not proof of execution: report branches and merges as completed only after verifying their actual refs and SHAs. These are agent instructions, not a technical lock on Git operations.

## The delivery loop

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User objective] --> P[Product owner clarifies intent]
    P --> O[Orchestrator plans and organizes]
    O --> W[Bounded workers]
    W --> R[Independent review]
    R -->|corrections| W
    R --> I[Integrate and verify exact revision]
    I --> O
    O --> M[Record meaningful transitions]
    M --> O
    O --> F[Report outcome and remaining gaps]
```

The loop is not a fixed waterfall. Work can move backward when evidence changes, but authorization, review, and exact-revision checks are not skipped.

### 1. Understand and organize

Read the request, relevant project state, and existing evidence. Establish observable success criteria, real dependencies, and useful execution units. Do not invent requirements when the project can answer them.

### 2. Prepare the workspace

For code-changing tasks, prepare `task/<id>` from the verified `development` head using the Git flow above. Sequential tasks may reuse a workspace only after preserving existing work and switching to the assigned task branch. Use separate worktrees for concurrent or conflicting work. Record the starting revision and keep one writer per branch and workspace; workers verify their assigned branch and SHA before changes.

### 3. Delegate

Choose `explore` for bounded read-only discovery and `general` when a worker must save a report; `explore` cannot write files.

Give each worker:

- the objective and acceptance examples;
- relevant findings and constraints;
- the workspace and starting revision when applicable;
- the exact scope and expected evidence;
- the safety and authorization limits that still apply.

Workers return a result, changes, checks tied to a revision, blockers, and evidence paths. They do not edit coordination state.

### 4. Validate and review

Check acceptance and real test evidence. A non-trivial change set needs an independent `code-reviewer` before integration or completion — including changes to logic, behavior, configuration, or agent instructions. Passing tests and implementer self-review do not replace independent review.

The reviewer receives the acceptance criteria, workspace, base and target revisions or working-tree scope, full diff, and test evidence. Confirmed blocking findings must be resolved or explicitly rejected with evidence.

### 5. Integrate incrementally

Integrate serially into `development`, preferably a fast-forward of a validated revision that includes its current head. Never force, reset, or overwrite another contributor's work. Re-run relevant checks after every synchronization, even when there are no conflicts. Verify task-tip ancestry and the resulting integrated revision before recording completion.

### 6. Finish

Verify the combined result against the user's objective. Report what was delivered, what was not, and any remaining uncertainty. Integration is not deployment.

## Delegation and sessions

Use a fresh session for each independent assignment. Reuse a session only for clarification, correction, synchronization, or validation of that same deliverable — not merely because the role, model, repository, or objective is the same.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Independent assignment] --> B[Fresh child session]
    B --> C[Bounded deliverable]
    C --> D{Correction or clarification?}
    D -- Yes --> B
    D -- No --> E[New independent assignment]
    E --> F[Fresh child session]
```

A useful worker handoff is short and evidence-based:

- result;
- changes;
- checks and the exact tested revision;
- blockers;
- evidence paths.

Detailed reports and logs stay in files. The handoff should not replay the whole investigation.

## Review and integration

Review is a gate, not a formality.

- Start a fresh reviewer for each independent change set.
- Review the actual diff, not only the implementer's summary.
- Separate correctness findings from optional polish.
- Reuse the original implementer and reviewer for corrections to that change set.
- Broaden the review if the design changes.
- Record the reviewer, reviewed revision or diff, findings, and disposition.

Checks attributed to a commit require that exact revision, with no staged, unstaged, or untracked code, tests, or configuration that could affect the result. Verify the revision and working-tree state before and after the checks. Use a clean validation worktree when existing changes would interfere.

## Workspaces

Temporary worktrees are part of delivery, not permanent project state. Release them incrementally when the associated work is genuinely finished.

Before removing a workspace:

1. verify every user of the directory has finished;
2. check running shells, background tools, and other processes;
3. preserve branches, recovery refs, and durable evidence outside the workspace;
4. move sessions to an existing checkout;
5. remove with a non-forcing strategy;
6. verify the resulting inventory and preserved refs.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active
    Active --> Retained: review or recovery still needs it
    Active --> Removed: all users finished and evidence preserved
    Retained --> Removed: dependency resolved
```

Unknown ownership, unknown activity, failed preservation, or unsafe removal behavior means **retain**, not force. A completed worker execution alone is not proof that the workspace is free: pending review, corrections, integration, or another background process may still need it.

## Coordination loop

For sustained work, `start-orchestrator-loop` enables a persistent reminder loop for the current root orchestrator session. The default interval is ten minutes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Timer as Scheduler
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant W as Workers
    participant M as Memory manager
    Timer->>O: Short coordination reminder
    O->>W: Inspect activity and results
    W-->>O: Evidence, blockers, next facts
    O->>M: Delegate meaningful transition
    M-->>O: Changed IDs, versions, curation decisions
    O->>O: Choose next useful action
```

The reminder asks the orchestrator to:

- inspect current worker and background activity;
- reconcile results, reviews, and blockers;
- update the backlog through the memory-manager;
- release eligible workspaces;
- advance the next useful action without waiting for another user prompt.

The reminder does not fetch or inject child inventories, repeat the stored objective, or automatically remove workspaces. It does not prove that work progressed. Delivery happens at a step boundary and may be delayed by a running model request or tool.

Use `orchestrator-status` when loop state or delivery is uncertain. It reports stored settings, the local scheduler, pending reminders, and delivery diagnostics without waking execution. A successful wake request is not proof that the reminder was processed.

Stop the loop when the objective is achieved or the user asks. Stopping cancels pending reminders; already delivered reminders and running worker tasks are not interrupted.

## Model configuration

Models are configured in the first existing file:

1. project `.opencode/orchestrator.md`;
2. `~/.config/opencode/orchestrator.md`.

```markdown
complex: provider/model-a#max, provider/model-b#xhigh
normal: provider/model-c
```

- A model reference is `provider/model`, optionally with a variant such as `#max` or `#xhigh`.
- Each level is a comma-separated pool. Round-robin is the default; the orchestrator may choose another configured model when useful.
- `complex` and `normal` apply across ticket kinds.
- Reviewers and simplifiers default to the orchestrator's session model.
- Missing `complex` uses `normal`; missing `normal` or no configuration uses the session model.
- Commit the project file for a team standard, or keep it local for personal preferences.

## Autonomy and authorization

Routine technical choices, ticket adjustments, scheduling, and recovery do not need renewed approval. The orchestrator adapts after failures rather than stopping at a fixed retry count.

Irreversible, destructive, or costly actions need clear authorization, even inside the objective. Existing authorization does not need to be repeated, but it must be real and must cover the action.

With `orchestrator` selected, say **“Automatic mode”** to delegate remaining choices for the established objective without routine confirmation. Automatic mode belongs only to the orchestrator; the product owner and workers do not inherit it.

## Common failure modes

| Failure | Correction |
|---|---|
| Reusing a session because the role matches | Start fresh unless it is the same deliverable |
| Treating a dispatched worker as a finished run | Wait for evidence and distinguish dispatch from execution |
| Relying on an implementer's summary | Review the diff and checks |
| Running checks on a different revision | Verify exact SHA and working-tree state |
| Keeping a workspace because a session is inactive | Check background users and evidence, then reconcile explicitly |
| Letting the orchestrator rewrite memory directly | Delegate the transition to the memory-manager |
| Recording a chronology in every ticket | Keep a current snapshot and link detailed evidence |
| Skipping review for agent/configuration changes | Review non-trivial changes of every kind |

### /diff-summary

The `/diff-summary` command supports two modes:

**Working tree mode** (no parameters):
```bash
/diff-summary
```
Shows staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked file contents.

**Branch comparison mode** (with parameters):
```bash
# Compare a branch with the current branch (HEAD)
/diff-summary feature-branch

# Compare two specific branches
/diff-summary feature-branch main
```
Shows stats overview, commits, files changed, and full diff between branches.

### /memory-review

Runs an on-demand global knowledge review in a read-only `memory-reviewer` child session. It uses the
read-only `memory-review` inventory, then reads all entries with `knowledge list/get`.
The result is a coverage summary and reasoned proposals, not applied changes. The user must
validate proposals before a separate manager pass can apply them. Tasks are read only for
context or reference checks. Tool-level identity checks reject reviewer mutations; it cannot
create backups or delegate. See [Project memory](memory.md#on-demand-global-review).

### /memory, /task-board, /knowledge

Read-only inspection commands. Each calls one tool and returns its Markdown output unchanged:
the tool formats, the model only relays. They never save or remove memory and never create
or upgrade a missing store.

- `/memory` reports the store path, task counts by status and a knowledge topic inventory through
  the read-only `memory-overview` tool.
- `/task-board` shows every task except `done` as columns in the order `todo`, `in-progress`,
  `review`, `blocked`, with `ID — Title` cells; `list <status>` filters (including `done`, also
  available as bare `done`), and `get <ID>` shows one task's current description and version.
- `/knowledge` lists topics, lists or searches entries, and `get <ID>` shows one entry.

Use `/memory-review` when the goal is to assess and propose changes, not merely to consult memory.

The underlying record tools also support `get` with `offset`, `limit` and a continuation
`version`, plus `history` (current + one previous version, or last saved content and a removal
token for deleted knowledge) and manager-only `restore`. Older versions are automatically
discarded. `memory-backup` creates a verified
standalone local backup without changing current records. These capabilities are accessed
through tools rather than additional slash-command arguments. See
[Recovery history and backups](memory.md#recovery-history-and-backups).

### /linear-stale-check

Analyzes open Linear issues for the team configured in `AGENTS.md` with:

```text
Linear team: <name>
```

If no team is configured, the command lists available Linear teams and asks which one to use for the current run.

The command is read-only. It fetches open issues, investigates related code, skips code investigation for issues already `In Progress`, and outputs a single report grouped by verdict:

- 🔴 Likely obsolete
- 🟡 Uncertain
- 🟢 Likely active

It does not modify Linear issues, add comments, or update project files.

## Skills

Skills are contextual instructions loaded on demand via the `skill` tool. The agent invokes `skill({ id: "skill-name" })` to load the instructions when needed.

### Overview

- Skills provide specialized guidance for specific tasks
- Instructions are loaded only when explicitly requested

### Available Skills

#### Example: ask-questions-if-underspecified

**Agent response (after loading the skill):**

The agent recognizes this request has multiple interpretations and uses the `question` tool:

┌─ Authentication Approach ────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                  │
│  Which authentication method should be implemented?              │
│                                                                  │
│  ○ JWT tokens (Recommended)                                      │
│  ○ Session-based with cookies                                    │

#### Example: tdd

**User request:**
> "Add a function to calculate the total price with tax"

**Agent response (after loading the skill):**

The agent follows the TDD workflow:

1. **Requirement Synthesis:**
> "I'll create a function that calculates total price with tax. It should accept a price and tax rate, returning the total."

2. **Red — test one behavior and run it to observe the expected failure:**
```typescript
describe("calculateTotalWithTax", () => {
  it("should add tax to the base price", () => {
    expect(calculateTotalWithTax(100, 0.2)).toBe(120)
  })
})
```

3. **Green — implement the minimum behavior and run the test again:**
```typescript
function calculateTotalWithTax(price: number, taxRate: number): number {
  return price * (1 + taxRate)
}
```

4. **Refactor:** simplify only where useful while preserving passing tests, then repeat for the next behavior (such as zero tax). Run relevant regression checks and report actual results. A pre-existing passing behavior needs verification, not an invented failure to manufacture a red phase.

### Discovery Locations

Skills are discovered from the following locations, in order of increasing priority:

| Priority | Scope | Location |
|----------|-------|----------|
| 1 (lowest) | plugin | `<plugin>/skill/` |
| 2 | global | `~/.config/opencode/skill/` |
| 3 (highest) | project | `<project>/.opencode/skill/` |

If multiple skills share the same name, the one from the highest-priority location takes precedence.

### Creating a Skill

Each skill lives in its own directory with a `SKILL.md` file:

```
skill/
└── my-skill/
    └── SKILL.md
```

The `SKILL.md` file uses YAML frontmatter for metadata:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: Short description of the skill (required)
use_when: >
  Condition for automatic activation (optional).
---

# Detailed Instructions

Markdown content with step-by-step guidance...
```

#### Frontmatter Fields

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | No | Identifier for the skill; defaults to the directory name |
| `description` | No | Short description (displayed in skill listings); may be empty |
| `use_when` | No | Condition for automatic activation |

A directory without `SKILL.md` is skipped. A `SKILL.md` without a `name` uses its directory name.

### Automatic Activation

If a skill defines `use_when`, a directive is injected into the system prompt:

```
MANDATORY: Call skill({ id: "my-skill" }) <use_when content>
```

This instructs the agent to load the skill when the specified condition is met.

**What is injected:**
- The skill `name`
- The `use_when` text (normalized: multiple spaces collapsed to single space)

**What is NOT injected:**
- The `description`
- The markdown content (loaded only when the skill is invoked)

### gitingest

Fetch a GitHub repository's full content via gitingest.com. Returns summary, directory tree, and file contents optimized for LLM analysis. Use when you need to understand an external repository's structure or code.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `url` | `string` | Yes | - | The GitHub repository URL to fetch |
| `maxFileSize` | `number` | No | `50000` | Maximum file size in bytes to include |
| `pattern` | `string` | No | `""` | Glob pattern to filter files (e.g., `*.ts`, `src/**/*.py`) |
| `patternType` | `"include"` \| `"exclude"` | No | `"exclude"` | Whether to include or exclude files matching the pattern |

#### Usage Examples

```typescript
// Fetch entire repository
gitingest({ url: "https://github.com/user/repo" })

// Only TypeScript files
gitingest({
  url: "https://github.com/user/repo",
  pattern: "*.ts",
  patternType: "include"
})

// Exclude test files
gitingest({
  url: "https://github.com/user/repo",
  pattern: "*.test.ts",
  patternType: "exclude"
})

// Increase max file size to 100KB
gitingest({
  url: "https://github.com/user/repo",
  maxFileSize: 100000
})
```

#### Limitations

- Content is truncated to 300k characters (server-side limit from gitingest.com)
- For large repositories, use pattern filtering to focus on relevant files
- The `maxFileSize` parameter controls individual file size, not total output size

### session-context

Use `/session-context [limit]` to analyze the most recent sessions in the current project, including subagent sessions. The command calls the `session-context` tool and asks the agent to return its Markdown table and category list. Raw session messages are read inside the tool process and are never returned or copied into the discussion.

The `session-context` tool returns a Markdown table by default, so the agent can render it directly in its response. Its result contains only aggregated metrics; it never includes raw messages. The tool adds its small schema to the agent's tool catalog.

For each row the report includes the agent type, model and variant, active-context size after the last compaction, the model context limit and usage, the top tool by characters, cumulative session tokens and cost, and a character-based breakdown by category.

`Context` is the last assistant prompt (`input + cache.read + cache.write`), not cumulative session input. `Used` is `Context / model limit`. Category percentages are shares of active context characters after the last compaction; they are not token shares and exclude tool-schema/system overhead that is not present in messages. Attachments are counted separately and excluded from percentages. Context messages include `system`, `user`, `assistant`, `reasoning`, `tool calls`, `tool results`, `compaction` and `other` (shell).

The `Tools` table aggregates tool-call input and tool-result characters per tool name across the analyzed sessions. Its share is over all tool characters, so it answers which tools consume the active context. Tool parts without a name are reported as `(unnamed)`. The table lists the top 10 tools by characters.

The tool reads session inventory through the OpenCode API and context/model data through the plugin host, after verifying that the CLI addresses the same service. It does not start, stop, modify or compact a session. A context failure is reported on its row without hiding other sessions. If model limits are unavailable, rows still render with `n/a` usage. This is read-only reporting, not live activity or task completion.

#### Parameters

| Entry point | Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|-------------|-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `/session-context` | `limit` | `integer` | No | `10` | Positional argument, from 1 to 50 |
| `session-context` tool | `limit` | `integer` | No | `10` | Number of recent sessions to analyze, from 1 to 50 |

#### Usage Examples

```text
/session-context
/session-context 5
```

The slash command and tool are the supported entry points. The standalone `froggy-session-context` CLI and its text report have been removed; no separate CLI install is needed.

#### Output

The tool returns a Markdown summary table followed by category and tool tables:

```markdown
| # | Session | Agent · Model | Context / Limit (used) | Top tool | Cost | Cumul session (in/out/cache) |
|---|---------|---------------|------------------------|----------|------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | Passe 7j… | memory-manager (sub) · deepseek/deepseek-flash#high | 242.5k / 1.00M (24.2%) | shell 220.9k | $2.58 | 6.18M / 1.38M / 112M |

### Categories

| # | Agent (kind) | Cost | reasoning | tool calls | tool results | system | compaction | assistant | user | other |
|---|--------------|------|-----------|------------|--------------|--------|------------|-----------|------|-------|
| 1 | memory-manager (sub) | $2.58 | 23.3% | 25.0% | 35.0% | 0.0% | 15.5% | 0.6% | 0.4% | 0.0% |
| **Global** | **all sessions** | **$2.58** | **23.3%** | **25.0%** | **35.0%** | **0.0%** | **15.5%** | **0.6%** | **0.4%** | **0.0%** |

### Tools

| Tool | Calls | Call chars | Result chars | Share of tool chars |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| shell | 120 | 40.1k | 220.9k | 52.0% |
```

`Context / Limit` is the last assistant prompt and its share of the model window. `Cumul session` is cumulative `input / output / cache read` for the whole session, separate from the active context. `Cost` is the session cost in USD. `Top tool` is the tool with the most characters in that session. The `Global` row shows the weighted category share across analyzed sessions and the total cost of the listed sessions.

### agent-promote

Promote an agent to primary (default) or specify a grade.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | `string` | Yes | Name of the plugin agent (e.g., `rubber-duck`, `architect`) |
| `grade` | `string` | No | Target type: `subagent`, `primary`, or `all` (default: `primary`) |

#### Grade Types

| Grade | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| `subagent` | Available only as a subagent |
| `primary` | Appears in Tab selection for direct use |
| `all` | Available both as primary and subagent |

#### Usage Examples

```bash
# Promote rubber-duck to primary (default)
/agent-promote rubber-duck

# Promote with explicit grade
/agent-promote architect all

# Demote back to subagent
/agent-demote rubber-duck
```

#### Notes

- Only agents from this plugin can be promoted (see the [Agents](../README.md#agents) table)
- Promotions and demotions are held only in memory for the current project's plugin instance (OpenCode location). Other projects and worktrees have independent instances; conversations in the same location share the mode.
- A registry refresh preserves the requested mode. Reloading the plugin or restarting OpenCode restores the modes defined in `agent/*.md`. Neither operation writes agent files or persistent promotion settings.
- The tool checks the effective mode after reloading. If a global/project agent definition or a later plugin overrides it, the tool reports the conflict instead of claiming success.

## Configuration

The plugin loads agents, commands, and skills automatically from the `agent/`, `command/`, and `skill/` directories.

Bundled agent definitions use V2 `permissions` arrays of `{ action, resource, effect }` rules. The plugin no longer converts legacy `permission`, `tools` or object-shaped permissions; unsupported formats fail explicitly instead of silently dropping restrictions. Global and project agent definitions remain managed by OpenCode.

Bundled commands are installed under `<config-home>/opencode/commands/`, and legacy agent copies are checked under `<config-home>/opencode/agents/`. On every platform, `<config-home>` is `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when set, otherwise `~/.config`.
